description: Between **1945** and **1946**, **24** Nazi leaders stood trial at Nuremberg. For the first time, an international court invented crimes against humanity.

hero.hook: Trying the defeated in order to invent international justice, not simply to take revenge.

blocks.text: From November **1945** to October **1946**, the German city of **Nuremberg**, once the showcase of the Nazis, hosted a court with no precedent. The Allies were not content with having won the war. They put the losers on trial.
The trial established one simple, radical idea: even a powerful leader can answer for his acts in court. It also made **[[crimes against humanity]]** a category of **[[international law]]**.

British Prime Minister **Winston Churchill** first thought of summary executions. **Joseph Stalin**, the leader of the USSR, preferred trials whose verdicts would be written in advance. The American line won out, argued by the jurist **Robert Jackson**: a real trial, with evidence and rights for the defense.

The **[[London Charter]]** (August **1945**) created the International Military Tribunal. There were four counts: conspiracy, crimes against peace, war crimes, and, for the first time, **[[crimes against humanity]]**.

blocks.caption: The dock at Nuremberg, facing the judges of the four Allied powers

blocks.text: Nuremberg was not chosen for its symbolism alone: it was one of the few German cities left with an intact courthouse and a prison joined to it by a tunnel.

Twenty-four defendants stood for the whole Nazi state. **Hermann Göring**, the former head of the **[[Luftwaffe]]** (the German air force), dominated the dock with his arrogance. **Albert Speer**, the armaments minister, admitted a share of the responsibility.

blocks.caption: Hermann Göring at the Nuremberg trials

blocks.text: Jackson relied above all on the Nazi archives themselves: millions of pages, photographs, appointment books. Another shock came from the films shot when the camps were liberated. The room went silent. This was no longer the trial of a defeat. It was the trial of a system.
On **October 1, 1946**, the verdict came: **12** death sentences, **3** life sentences, **4** prison terms, **3** acquittals. There was no automatic conviction. Individual guilt counted.

The **[[Nuremberg Principles]]** hold that obeying a superior does not wash away a crime. Later came the tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and for Rwanda, then the **[[International Criminal Court]]** (**2002**).
Göring killed himself the night before his execution with a cyanide capsule. How he got hold of it has never been fully explained.

Critics attacked the break with **[[non-retroactivity]]**: judging crimes that no prewar law code named. And the absence of any judgment on Allied crimes, such as the massacre at **[[Katyn]]** (Polish officers killed by the Soviets in **1940**), fed the idea of a justice with double standards.
Even so, Nuremberg fixed a historical record that is hard to deny, and prepared the Universal Declaration of Human Rights of **1948**: even a powerful state does not stand above the law.
Nuremberg (**1945-1946**) invented **[[crimes against humanity]]** and established that a leader can be tried as an individual by an international court.
